items.a_text: Alcohol consumption shows differing risk associations by stroke subtype, with a lower risk for incident ischaemic stroke (RR 0.92, 95% CI 0.85 to 1.00) and an elevated risk for incident haemorrhagic stroke (RR 1.14, 95% CI 0.97 to 1.34).
items.b_text: Higher alcohol consumption is roughly linearly associated with a higher risk of stroke (HR 1.14 per 100 g/week higher consumption).
items.explanation: Claim A examines risk associations for specific stroke subtypes, whereas Claim B assesses the overall linear risk of total stroke relative to alcohol intake.

items.a_text: Alcohol consumption exhibits a curvilinear J-shaped dose-response relationship with the relative risk of ischemic stroke.
items.b_text: Alcohol consumption is not significantly associated with overall incident stroke compared with non-drinking (pooled adjusted RR 0.98, 95% CI 0.91 to 1.06).
items.explanation: Claim A refers specifically to a non-linear dose-response relationship with ischemic stroke, while Claim B evaluates the overall risk across all stroke types compared to non-drinking.

items.a_text: Processed meat consumption is not associated with incident stroke.
items.b_text: Consumption of 100 g/day of unprocessed red meat is associated with an 11% increased risk of stroke.
items.explanation: The claims evaluate different types of meat (processed meat versus unprocessed red meat), so they refer to distinct constructs.

items.a_text: Intake of whole grain is inversely related to cardiovascular disease.
items.b_text: Increased intake of whole grains is inversely associated with type 2 diabetes incidence.
items.explanation: While both claims indicate health benefits from whole grain intake, they address different medical outcomes: cardiovascular disease and type 2 diabetes.

items.a_text: No single type of alcoholic beverage conferred an additional risk reduction for myocardial infarction beyond drinking frequency.
items.b_text: Increased alcohol consumption is log-linearly associated with a lower risk of myocardial infarction (HR 0.94 per 100 g/week higher consumption).
items.explanation: Claim A addresses whether the type of alcoholic beverage provides additional risk reduction for myocardial infarction beyond drinking frequency, whereas Claim B focuses on the quantitative association between total alcohol intake and myocardial infarction risk.

items.a_text: Processed meat intake is associated with a 42% higher risk of incident coronary heart disease per 50-g serving per day.
items.b_text: Consumption of 50 g/day of processed meat is associated with a 32% increased risk of diabetes.
items.explanation: The claims examine the association of processed meat consumption with two distinct health outcomes—coronary heart disease and diabetes—making them neither mutually supporting nor contradictory.

items.a_text: Intake of whole grain is inversely related to obesity.
items.b_text: Increased intake of whole grains is inversely associated with type 2 diabetes incidence.
items.explanation: The claims examine different health outcomes associated with whole grain intake, specifically obesity versus type 2 diabetes incidence.

items.a_text: Unprocessed red meat intake is not associated with incident coronary heart disease.
items.b_text: Consumption of 100 g/day of unprocessed red meat is associated with a 15% increased risk of cardiovascular mortality.
items.explanation: Claim A evaluates incident coronary heart disease while Claim B focuses on cardiovascular mortality, representing distinct health outcomes that neither directly support nor contradict each other.

items.a_text: Alcohol consumption is associated with a lower risk of incident coronary heart disease compared with non-drinking (pooled adjusted RR 0.71, 95% CI 0.66 to 0.77).
items.b_text: Higher alcohol consumption is roughly linearly associated with a higher risk of coronary disease excluding myocardial infarction (HR 1.06 per 100 g/week higher consumption).
items.explanation: The claims examine different specific endpoints and comparisons, with one comparing overall alcohol drinkers to non-drinkers for total incident coronary heart disease and the other evaluating a linear dose-response for coronary disease excluding myocardial infarction.

items.a_text: Alcohol consumption is associated with a lower risk of all-cause mortality compared with non-drinking (pooled adjusted RR 0.87, 95% CI 0.83 to 0.92).
items.b_text: Estimates of all-cause mortality risk from alcohol consumption are significantly altered by study design and quality characteristics.
items.explanation: Claim A provides a specific estimate for the association between alcohol consumption and all-cause mortality, while Claim B discusses how study design and quality affect such risk estimates in general.

items.a_text: Intake of whole grain is inversely related to cancer.
items.b_text: Increased intake of whole grains is inversely associated with type 2 diabetes incidence.
items.explanation: The claims discuss the effect of whole grain intake on two different health outcomes, cancer and type 2 diabetes, making them neither supporting nor contradicting.

items.a_text: Reducing saturated fat intake has little or no effect on cardiovascular mortality.
items.b_text: Saturated fatty acid reduction has little direct effect on stroke risk.
items.explanation: Although both claims suggest that reducing saturated fat intake has minimal impact, they address distinct health outcomes: cardiovascular mortality and stroke risk.

items.a_text: The NAFLD Fibrosis Score achieves an AUROC of 0.85 for predicting advanced fibrosis in patients with NAFLD.
items.b_text: Advanced fibrosis in NAFLD refers specifically to stage 3 bridging fibrosis or stage 4 cirrhosis.
items.explanation: Claim A reports the predictive accuracy of a diagnostic score, whereas Claim B provides a definition of advanced fibrosis in NAFLD.

items.a_text: Alcohol consumption is associated with a lower risk of coronary heart disease mortality compared with non-drinking (pooled adjusted RR 0.75, 95% CI 0.68 to 0.81).
items.b_text: Higher alcohol consumption is roughly linearly associated with a higher risk of coronary disease excluding myocardial infarction (HR 1.06 per 100 g/week higher consumption).
items.explanation: The claims evaluate different outcomes and comparisons, with one examining coronary heart disease mortality between drinkers and non-drinkers and the other examining the dose-response relationship of alcohol consumption on coronary disease excluding myocardial infarction.

items.a_text: The decreased risk of myocardial infarction was similar between men consuming less than 10 g of alcohol per drinking day and those consuming 30 g or more.
items.b_text: Cardiovascular disease death rates were 30 to 40 percent lower among men reporting at least one drink daily compared with nondrinkers.
items.explanation: Claim A compares different levels of alcohol intake regarding myocardial infarction risk, while Claim B compares drinkers to nondrinkers regarding cardiovascular disease mortality.

items.a_text: For women, the relative risk of alcohol consumption on stroke differs significantly when comparing mortality endpoints to morbidity endpoints.
items.b_text: Alcohol consumption is not significantly associated with overall incident stroke compared with non-drinking (pooled adjusted RR 0.98, 95% CI 0.91 to 1.06).
items.explanation: Claim A addresses differences between mortality and morbidity endpoints in women specifically, whereas Claim B provides a pooled overall association for incident stroke.

items.a_text: Substituting 3% of energy from plant protein for protein from unprocessed red meat was associated with lower all-cause mortality.

items.b_text: Greater dose-response exposure to ultra-processed foods is directly associated with a higher risk of incident type 2 diabetes (risk ratio 1.12, 95% confidence interval 1.11 to 1.13).
items.explanation: The claims evaluate distinct dietary exposures—an unhealthful plant-based diet index versus ultra-processed food consumption—in relation to type 2 diabetes risk.
